nameStory: The Scalyleg Mite gets its descriptive name from what it does to its victims - it burrows under the scales of bird legs and feet, causing them to lift up and create a rough, scaly appearance. This tiny troublemaker literally makes legs look scaly, so the name tells the whole story of its impact on backyard birds.
description: The Scalyleg Mite is a microscopic arachnid that's practically invisible to the naked eye, measuring less than half a millimeter long. These tiny parasites are oval-shaped and pale, living their entire lives burrowing beneath the scales on bird feet and legs. You'll never see the mite itself during casual observation, but you'll definitely notice the crusty, thickened scales and rough texture they create on infected birds. They're part of the same group of mites that cause scabies in mammals.

idTips.label: Size

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Tiny oval body that's pale whitish or translucent when viewed under magnification

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Lives by burrowing tunnels under bird leg scales, never free-living on surfaces

idTips.label: Signs
idTips.description: Look for thickened, crusty, raised scales on bird feet that feel rough and bumpy to touch

idTips.label: Location
idTips.description: Found exclusively on birds, particularly on unfeathered legs, feet, and toes

habitat: You won't find these mites crawling around in nature - they live exclusively on birds throughout New England. They're most commonly encountered on backyard chickens, wild turkeys, and other ground-dwelling birds that visit feeders or roost in barns and coops. The mites prefer the unfeathered portions of bird legs where they can easily burrow under scales.

seasonality.spring: Mite populations begin building as birds become more active and social during nesting season, making transmission more likely between individuals.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when warm weather allows mite reproduction to accelerate, and infected birds show the most obvious scaly leg symptoms.
seasonality.fall: Mite infestations often become most noticeable as birds gather in flocks for migration or winter roosting, spreading the parasites.
seasonality.winter: Mites remain active even in cold weather since they live in the warm environment under bird scales, continuing to cause thickened, crusty feet.

funFact: These mites are so tiny that hundreds of them can live in the space under a single bird scale, creating intricate tunnel systems like microscopic mining operations that gradually push the scales upward and outward!
confusionNotes: The scaly, thickened appearance on bird legs is sometimes mistaken for a fungal infection or natural aging, but fungal problems usually cause softer, flaky skin while mite damage creates hard, raised scales that feel distinctly bumpy and crusty to the touch.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Scalyleg Mite' in common usage, this same species also causes 'scaly foot' - both names refer to the same condition caused by the same mite. Backyard chicken keepers are most likely to encounter this species, though it affects wild birds too.
compareHints: As the only member of its genus recorded in New England, the Scalyleg Mite is unique among local arachnids for its exclusive bird-parasitic lifestyle. Unlike other mites that might occasionally be found on birds, this species never lives anywhere else and creates the distinctive tunnel-and-scale-lifting behavior that no other regional mite exhibits.
